items.title: Today's lesson
items.content:
A cab-ride puzzle opens the difference between **distance** and **displacement**.

One running-track example then carries the whole lesson: position, distance, displacement, speed and velocity are all read off the same picture.

We finish with exam-style numericals.

items.title: You already know
items.content:
• speed = distance ÷ time

• reading **+** and **−** values on a number line

items.title: By the end, you can
items.content:
**1.** Describe a position using a reference point, and tell distance apart from displacement.

**2.** Find average speed and average velocity, with their SI units.

**3.** Tell uniform motion from non-uniform motion.

**4.** Solve numericals on speed and velocity.

items.text:
**What this screen shows**

• A map of your trip from **Home** to the **Railway Station**.

• The path the cab actually took is **8 km**.

• The direct path between the two is just **3 km**.

**Answer to Question 1**

8 km — the path it actually drove.

**Answer to Question 2**

How far the Railway Station is from Home, in a straight line.

**Answer to Question 3**

16 km travelled in total — but you are 0 km from where you started.

**What this shows**

• An athlete is running on this straight **100 m** track.

• **O** is the reference point; **B** is at 40 m and **A** is at 100 m.

• Right of O is the **+ direction**, left of O is the **− direction**.

**Answer to Question 4**

No. 40 m from where, and which way? A distance on its own does not fix a position.

chunks.name: To give a position, three things

items.text:
**What this shows**

• An athlete is running on this straight **100 m** track.

• **O** is the reference point; **B** is at 40 m and **A** is at 100 m.

• Right of O is the **+ direction**, left of O is the **− direction**.

**Answer to Question 5**

20 m to the left of O, so her position is −20 m.

**Answer to Question 6**

At rest compared with the train; in motion compared with the platform.

items.text:
**What this shows**

• A straight 100 m track, drawn as a number line with **O** as the reference point.

• She starts at **O**, passes **B** at t = 4 s and reaches **A** at t = 10 s.

• She then turns back and stops at **B** at t = 16 s.

**Answer to Question 7**

$100\ \text{m} + 60\ \text{m} = 160\ \text{m}$

This is the **distance**.

**Answer to Question 8**

$+40\ \text{m}$, in the positive direction.

This is the **displacement**.

Question 7, then Question 8. Answers are on pointers 2 and 3.

chunks.name: The same run, looked at again

items.text:
**What this shows**

• A straight 100 m track, drawn as a number line with **O** as the reference point.

• She starts at **O**, passes **B** at t = 4 s and reaches **A** at t = 10 s.

• She then turns back and stops at **B** at t = 16 s.

**Answer to Question 9**

$\text{distance} = 100\ \text{m}$

$\text{displacement} = +100\ \text{m}$

Here the distance equals the magnitude of the displacement.

items.prompt: A ball is thrown 60 cm straight up and falls back into the same hand. Distance travelled and displacement?
options: 0 cm, 0 cm
60 cm, 0 cm
120 cm, 0 cm

items.prompt: Assertion (A): Displacement can be greater in magnitude than the distance travelled.  Reason (R): Displacement is measured in a straight line from the start to the finish.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

items.prompt: In the athlete's run, where is she when her displacement is zero, and what is her distance travelled then?
options: At A — 100 m
At B — 160 m
Back at O — 200 m
Back at O — 0 m

items.text:
**On Question 2**

The straight line is the shortest path between two points, so displacement can never exceed distance. **A is false, R is true.**

script.x: Activate each question and explain depending on time available.
Pointer 1 carries the reasoning for Question 2.

items.text:
**Answer to Question 10**

Two ways.

**Speed** uses the distance:

$$\text{speed}=\frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$$
**Velocity** uses the displacement, so it also carries a direction:

$$\text{velocity}=\frac{\text{displacement}}{\text{time}}$$

script.x: Ask Question 10 and take answers. Answer is on pointer 1.
Show the key idea box with the two formulas.

items.text:
**What this shows**

• The same run as before: out from **O** to **A**, then back to **B**.

• Distance travelled = **160 m**; displacement = **+40 m**.

• The whole run took **16 s**.

**Answer to Question 11**

$$\frac{160\ \text{m}}{16\ \text{s}} = 10\ \text{m/s}$$

**Answer to Question 12**

$$\frac{+40\ \text{m}}{16\ \text{s}} = 2.5\ \text{m/s}$$

in the positive direction.

script.x: Bring the run back up. Pointer 1 if they need the numbers again.
Question 11, then Question 12. Answers are on pointers 2 and 3.

items.text:
**What this shows**

• A **25 m** pool, seen from above.

• Sarang swims from the start to the far end, then back to the start.

• The whole swim takes **50 s**.

**Answer to Question 13**

He swims $25 + 25 = 50\ \text{m}$ in $50\ \text{s}$.

$$\frac{50\ \text{m}}{50\ \text{s}} = 1\ \text{m/s}$$

**Answer to Question 14**

He finishes where he started, so his displacement is $0\ \text{m}$.

$$\frac{0\ \text{m}}{50\ \text{s}} = 0\ \text{m/s}$$

items.prompt: Under which condition is an object's average velocity zero while its average speed is not zero?
options: It moves in one direction at constant speed
It returns to its starting point
It stays at rest
It speeds up in one direction

items.prompt: Can an object have zero average speed but a non-zero average velocity?
options: Yes — if it returns to the start
Yes — if it moves slowly enough
No — zero speed means no distance, so no displacement
No — speed and velocity are unrelated

items.text:
**On Question 2**

A non-zero velocity needs a non-zero displacement, and any displacement means some distance was covered — so the speed cannot be zero.

items.text:
**What this shows**

• Two cars, **P** and **Q**, driving along a straight road.

• Each row is one second of the journey.

• The number is the distance that car covered during that second.

**Answer to Question 15**

**Car P** — it covers $10\ \text{m}$ in every second.

**Answer to Question 16**

**Car Q** is covering more ground every second ($2, 6, 10, 14\ \text{m}$), so it is **speeding up**.

Question 15, then Question 16. Answers are on pointers 2 and 3.

items.prompt: A cyclist covers 20 m, 20 m, 20 m and 20 m in four successive 5 s intervals. A runner covers 15 m, 25 m, 25 m and 10 m in the same intervals. Whose motion is non-uniform?
options: The cyclist's
The runner's
Both of them
Neither of them

items.prompt: Assertion (A): A car that covers 40 km in every hour of a journey must be in uniform motion.  Reason (R): In uniform motion an object covers equal distances in equal intervals of time, for all choices of intervals.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

items.text:
**On Question 2**

Equal distances per hour do not guarantee equal distances in every smaller interval — the car could speed up and slow down within each hour. **A is false, R is true.**
